cards.headline: The printing press made ideas cheap
lines: Around 1450 in Mainz, Johannes Gutenberg combined movable metal type with a press.
Books became far cheaper; millions of copies were printed in Europe by 1500.
Cheap print helped spread the Reformation and the Scientific Revolution.
cards.source: Eisenstein, 'The Printing Revolution in Early Modern Europe' (1983).

cards.headline: Farming changed everything
lines: Around 10,000 years ago, people in the Fertile Crescent began farming wheat and barley.
Food surpluses allowed permanent villages, then towns, specialists and writing.
Farming arose independently in several places, including China, Mesoamerica and the Andes.
cards.source: Bellwood, 'First Farmers' (2005); Diamond, 'Guns, Germs, and Steel' (1997).

cards.headline: Writing began as bookkeeping
lines: The earliest known writing, Sumerian cuneiform in Mesopotamia, appeared around 3200 BCE.
Many early tablets are records of grain, livestock and labour.
Writing was also invented separately in China and in Mesoamerica.
cards.source: Schmandt-Besserat, 'How Writing Came About' (1996); Robinson, 'The Story of Writing'.

cards.headline: The Black Death reshaped Europe
lines: Between 1347 and 1351, plague killed roughly a third to a half of Europe's population.
With fewer workers, surviving labourers could demand higher wages.
Historians link it to the decline of serfdom in Western Europe.
cards.source: Benedictow, 'The Black Death 1346–1353' (2004); Herlihy, 'The Black Death and the Transformation of the West'.

cards.headline: The Industrial Revolution began in Britain
lines: From about 1760, machines, steam power and factories transformed how goods were made.
Coal, iron and cotton textiles led the way.
Over time it raised living standards — after decades of harsh working conditions.
cards.source: Allen, 'The British Industrial Revolution in Global Perspective' (2009).

cards.question: In which year is the Western Roman Empire traditionally said to have fallen?
cards.why: In 476 the last western emperor, Romulus Augustulus, was deposed. The Eastern (Byzantine) Empire lasted until 1453.
cards.source: Gibbon, 'The Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire'; Heather, 'The Fall of the Roman Empire' (2005).

cards.question: What principle is Magna Carta (1215) famous for?
options: The king is subject to the law
cards.why: It limited the king's power and became a symbol of the rule of law — though at the time it mainly protected the barons.

cards.question: Who brought movable-type printing to Europe around 1450?
cards.why: Gutenberg, in Mainz. Movable type existed earlier in China and Korea, but his press transformed Europe.
cards.source: Eisenstein, 'The Printing Revolution in Early Modern Europe' (1983).

cards.question: In which year did the Berlin Wall fall?
cards.why: The border opened on 9 November 1989. Germany reunified in 1990; the Soviet Union dissolved in 1991.
cards.source: Sarotte, 'The Collapse: The Accidental Opening of the Berlin Wall' (2014).

cards.question: The Great Pyramid of Giza was built for which pharaoh?
cards.why: Khufu, around 2560 BCE. It was the tallest human-made structure for nearly 4,000 years.

cards.headline: Cleopatra lived closer to the Moon landing than to the Great Pyramid
cards.text: The Great Pyramid dates to about 2560 BCE. Cleopatra died in 30 BCE — about 2,500 years later, and about 2,000 years before 1969.
cards.source: Lehner, 'The Complete Pyramids'; standard chronologies of Ptolemaic Egypt.

cards.headline: Oxford University is older than the Aztec capital
cards.text: Teaching was under way at Oxford by 1096. Tenochtitlan, the Aztec capital, was founded in 1325.
cards.source: University of Oxford, history of the university; Smith, 'The Aztecs' (3rd ed.).

cards.headline: Korea printed with metal type before Gutenberg
cards.text: The Jikji, printed in Korea in 1377, is the oldest surviving book printed with movable metal type.
cards.source: UNESCO Memory of the World Register, 'Baegun hwasang chorok buljo jikji simche yojeol' (vol. II).

cards.headline: The shortest recorded war lasted under an hour
cards.text: The Anglo-Zanzibar War of 27 August 1896 ended after roughly 38 to 45 minutes.

cards.headline: The Silk Roads

steps.headline: 1 · A network, not a road
lines: Land and sea routes linked China, Central Asia, India, the Middle East and Europe.
They flourished from about the 2nd century BCE.

steps.headline: 2 · More than silk
lines: Traders carried silk, spices, glass, horses and paper.
Few merchants travelled the whole way; goods passed from hand to hand.

steps.headline: 3 · Ideas travelled too
lines: Buddhism spread from India into China along these routes.
Papermaking moved west from China to the Islamic world, and on to Europe.

steps.headline: 4 · And so did disease
lines: Trade links also carried plague.
The Black Death most likely spread west along these routes in the 1340s.

cards.source: Frankopan, 'The Silk Roads' (2015); Hansen, 'The Silk Road: A New History' (2012).

cards.headline: History: the takeaways
points: Writing began as record-keeping in Sumer.
Printing made ideas cheap and fast.
The Black Death reshaped work in Europe.
Steam and factories began in 1700s Britain.
